# FAIR Data and Code Sharing {#sec-fairdata}

The Center for Open Science has announced that from November 16, 2026, no new projects can be created on the Open Science Framework (OSF). After February 19, all projects will become read-only, and eventually all private projects are expected to be deleted. The OSF has raised a generation of scientists able to practice open science, and these scientists will need to take these skills to a new data repository.

Before comparing alternatives, it is worth being clear that the fact that organizations are willing to store your data for free, for a very long time, is a remarkable service. Some common data repositories used in psychology are Zenodo, GitHub, ResearchBox, Dataverse, and PsychArchives. Below, these are compared on several properties that matter when choosing where to archive your data and code: longevity, API support, metadata, support for anonymous peer review, usability, and GDPR compliance.

## Longevity

Nothing lasts forever, but it helps if a data repository keeps going for a while. Zenodo is hosted by CERN and commissioned by the European Commission through the OpenAIRE project. CERN has existed since 1954, and will likely exist for a very long time. GitHub is owned by Microsoft (since 2018), and is unlikely to disappear soon. PsychArchives is hosted by ZPID, which started in 1971. The first Dataverse repository was hosted by Harvard in 2006 — Dataverse is not a single repository but open-source software run independently by many institutions, such as Harvard Dataverse and DataverseNL. The OSF started in 2013, hosted by the Center for Open Science. ResearchBox started in 2020, hosted by the Wharton Credibility Lab.

Predicting the future is difficult, but the order above roughly reflects likely longevity. As [the team behind ResearchBox explains](https://datacolada.org/137), they set up their system to minimize misuse, but running costs will continue to grow as more researchers start using the platform. All these services are likely to persist for at least the next decade. ResearchBox uses Zenodo as one of its long-term back-up solutions.

## API access

Data and code sharing is done as much for re-use by people as for re-use by machines. To enable machine re-use, a platform needs a good API (Application Programming Interface). GitHub, Zenodo, and Dataverse all have good APIs. The OSF has a usable API, but it is not well-designed and requires effort to use. PsychArchives has an API, but it is undocumented, so using it requires discovering it yourself; in addition, files shared under restrictive licenses on PsychArchives can be downloaded manually but not by software.

ResearchBox has no API at all. This is its biggest weakness, serious enough that it currently prevents recommending ResearchBox as a primary OSF alternative — even though it scores well on other dimensions. It is possible to scrape the ResearchBox website, but this is not a robust long-term solution.

Dataverse is open-source repository software rather than a single service — it is run independently by many institutions (e.g., Harvard Dataverse, DataverseNL, and various university-hosted installations), each on its own domain. They share the same API, but a tool first needs to recognize which specific Dataverse installation a given link belongs to, which adds some complexity compared to other services.

## Metadata

Metadata is how re-users find your data and code when they are not arriving via a link in a paper, which makes it important even though it can feel like a tedious detail. On the OSF, a project carries a title, description, a controlled category (e.g., project, data, hypothesis, methods and measures, software), an optional custom citation, free-form tags, a license, a discipline classification, and contributors — relatively limited compared to other repositories.

Zenodo's metadata model is richer and more structured for citation purposes: alongside title, description, and creators (name, affiliation, ORCID, GND), a deposit requires an upload type (e.g., publication, dataset, software, poster) and, for publications, a publication type (e.g., journal article, preprint, report, thesis). It supports free-form keywords and a controlled access right (open, embargoed, restricted, closed) with an associated license or embargo date. It also has related identifiers linking a deposit to other DOIs with a typed relationship (e.g., isSupplementTo, cites, isNewVersionOf), plus contributors distinct from creators, and grants that link a deposit to a funder-registered grant ID.

Dataverse goes further still, placing strong emphasis on structured, repository-level metadata that supports discovery, citation, and interoperability. Each dataset is described through a citation metadata block with fields such as title, author, contact, description, subject classification, keywords, producer, distributor, publication date, and related publications. Dataverse installations can also enable domain-specific metadata schemas (social science, geospatial, life science, astronomy), and datasets receive persistent identifiers (typically DOIs), versioning metadata, and machine-readable exports in standards such as Dublin Core and DataCite.

PsychArchives follows a metadata model designed around the needs of psychological science and the FAIR principles. Deposits are assigned DOIs and can represent articles, preprints, datasets, code, preregistrations, tests, and multimedia content. Metadata fields support detailed descriptions of authorship, affiliations, object type, publication status, licensing, keywords, and links between related outputs from the same study. Because PsychArchives is embedded in the ZPID ecosystem, metadata are also optimized for indexing by services such as PsychPorta and Google Scholar.

ResearchBox prioritizes usability and transparency for people browsing the website over highly formalized archival description. Public deposits are organized into standardized "Bingo Tables" indicating which components are available (preregistrations, materials, datasets, code, manuscripts). ResearchBox automatically generates dataset codebooks and supports searching within datasets, variable descriptions, and code files — making metadata partly file-derived rather than solely author-supplied. This is a genuinely good idea other repositories could learn from: FAIR metadata is much more achievable if most of it is generated automatically rather than entered by hand. Because there is no API, however, this metadata can currently only be searched manually on the website.

## Anonymous peer review

Many journals still require anonymous peer review. PsychArchives, ResearchBox, and the OSF all make it possible to share an anonymous link to data files for review. GitHub repositories can be anonymized for blind review using [anonymous.4open.science](https://anonymous.4open.science). Zenodo allows you to create a new upload, keep it private, fill in metadata without disclosing personal information, and then create a secret "can preview draft" link without publishing the record — reviewers can access the unpublished draft while it remains invisible to the public. Dataverse offers a more automated version: from an unpublished draft dataset, selecting Edit then Preview URL offers both a "General Preview URL" (comparable to Zenodo's secret link) and an "Anonymous Preview URL" that automatically strips author names and other identifying information from the citation, version history, and metadata, rather than relying on the depositor to avoid entering identifying information in the first place.

All platforms allow anonymous access to files, but ResearchBox, OSF, and PsychArchives make it easiest. Dataverse accommodates it well; it takes some getting used to on Zenodo; and it is hacky but possible on GitHub.

## Usability

A data sharing platform needs to do two things well: make it easy to upload and share data, and make it easy for others to find and download it. A recurring complaint about the OSF was that its user experience got in the way of sharing and re-use. For manual uploads, ResearchBox and PsychArchives offer a noticeably smoother experience, with ResearchBox in particular optimized for ease of use. Dataverse and Zenodo are also reasonably intuitive but more bare-bones — Zenodo, for instance, does not support folders, so all files are uploaded in a flat structure and you need file naming conventions or zip files to stay organized. GitHub requires more of a learning investment, and the biggest conceptual difference is that you are not meant to interact with it directly through a website — instead you use software (RStudio's Git pane, GitHub Desktop, or the command line) to push and pull files.

When it comes to finding files, ResearchBox has the most useful search: it can search inside data and code files, not just filenames, although this is only possible manually since there is no API. Dataverse also allows searching inside tabular data — for example, searching for "PANAS" to find datasets containing data from the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule — and this search is available through Dataverse's API. Other platforms generally only allow searching variable names and metadata.

Manual, first-order usability of a website matters, but programmatic, second-order access arguably matters more in the long run. Researchers will likely never browse repositories one by one to find relevant datasets; instead, search tools will crawl and index across repositories, which requires those repositories to have a good API. It is also increasingly easy to build a custom interface on top of an existing repository's API — an example for the OSF is [BetterOSF](https://betterosf.vercel.app/) by Gilad Feldman — but again, this depends entirely on the repository exposing a usable API.

## GDPR compliance

For fully anonymized data, the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) does not apply, and the data can be stored anywhere. Most research data, however, is pseudonymous: even if a shared file contains no directly identifying information, if a participant ID in that file could in principle be linked back to an email address or other identifying information held elsewhere (e.g., in a separate consent record), the data counts as pseudonymized under the GDPR.

Sharing pseudonymized data outside the EU generally requires that the repository be Data Privacy Framework certified, or that a Standard Contractual Clauses agreement is in place, or that the pseudonymization procedure is documented and formally approved by a national supervisory authority, with participants informed accordingly. Sharing anonymized data on Harvard Dataverse or ResearchBox is straightforward; sharing pseudonymized data is not.

Zenodo is a particularly important case here. Although CERN is located in Geneva, CERN is an international organization with special legal status under international law, and as a result [it is not subject to the GDPR](https://blog.zenodo.org/2018/05/25/2018-05-25-gdpr/). CERN instead processes personal data under its own internal framework, which it describes as built to the same standard as the GDPR without being a legal GDPR obligation. In practice, this means it is not legally possible to share pseudonymized data with Zenodo under the GDPR — Zenodo explicitly states it cannot sign [data processing agreements](https://support.zenodo.org/help/en-gb/32-data-privacy/148-can-we-conclude-a-data-processing-agreement-dpas-with-zenodo), and explicitly recommends other repositories [for data that originated from or contains sensitive personal data](https://help.zenodo.org/guides/nih/element5/). This is a legal quirk that applies to international organizations generally (see [this discussion](https://www.ejiltalk.org/with-whom-can-i-share-data-applying-the-gdpr-to-transfers-of-data-to-international-organisations/)) — Zenodo cannot be "GDPR compliant" for pseudonymized data because the GDPR simply does not apply to it, regardless of how good its data protection practices are otherwise.

The most straightforward way to stay GDPR compliant for pseudonymized data is to use PsychArchives or DataverseNL (both squarely GDPR compliant, being EU-based), or another local repository you may have institutional access to (for example, the [4TU.Research.Data repository](https://data.4tu.nl/) in the Netherlands). The downside is that research data can then end up distributed across many local repositories, each with its own rules and standards, making it harder to find and integrate data across a field.

## Choosing a repository

We currently live in a time where researchers can freely choose among several well-maintained repositories for storing research data — a genuinely fortunate position to be in, and one worth being grateful for given how recent this infrastructure is. The existence of multiple platforms also means they can learn from each other. This is part of why ResearchBox already gets so much right: as the newest entrant, it could learn from and improve on existing repositories. Its lack of an API remains a serious limitation, though, and PsychArchives would similarly benefit from documenting its API and allowing programmatic access to restricted files.

Dataverse and PsychArchives currently support metadata most systematically, following standards such as [Dublin Core](https://www.dublincore.org/). Repositories that support such standards will likely prove more useful a decade from now than those that do not — though metadata can also simply live as a standalone JSON file shared alongside the data, similar to how a README file is currently recommended, which somewhat reduces the importance of a repository's native metadata standard.

The best choice also depends on your own workflow. If you interact with the internet mainly by pointing and clicking, ResearchBox and PsychArchives will feel more comfortable than GitHub. If you interact with the internet through R or Python, Zenodo, Dataverse, or GitHub are the more natural fits. If your data is pseudonymized, Zenodo cannot formally be GDPR compliant — you either need to make the data fully anonymous (which makes data provenance harder, and is not always desirable) or use a GDPR-compliant repository such as DataverseNL or PsychArchives.

In summary, for **programmatic users** (R/Python), Zenodo, Dataverse, or GitHub are reasonable defaults; for **point-and-click users**, ResearchBox or PsychArchives are more approachable; for **pseudonymized data**, a GDPR-compliant repository (PsychArchives, DataverseNL, or a local institutional repository) is needed; and for **anonymized data accompanied by code**, Zenodo combined with a GitHub release is a common and effective combination.

It is worth closing with some appreciation for what the OSF achieved. It scored well on GDPR compliance, had a decent (if imperfect) API, and made anonymous peer review straightforward. Its usability could have been better, but for many projects it worked well enough. Larger alternative platforms such as Zenodo, GitHub, and Dataverse existed throughout this period too, but it was the OSF that managed to convince a generation of researchers in the social sciences to actually share data, code, and materials in the first place. That is a substantial accomplishment, and if researchers now move on to other platforms, it is in large part because the OSF got them started practicing open science to begin with.

## Making data and code machine readable

The [European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity](https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/docs/2021-2027/horizon/guidance/european-code-of-conduct-for-research-integrity_horizon_en.pdf) requires that data be shared "as open as possible, as closed as necessary," and in line with the FAIR principles: Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable. In practice, a person will rarely browse your files by hand — data and code are far more often found and reused through a search engine or downloaded automatically by a script. That means the real audience for how you organize a repository is often a machine, not a human, and it is worth following a few concrete practices that make automated reuse possible.

Keep repositories as small as reasonably possible. A script that downloads linked data from many papers at once will not cope well with repositories that are many gigabytes in size, and most of that bulk is often not needed to reproduce the reported results (e.g., raw stimulus materials, or intermediate output files that code can regenerate). As a rule of thumb, try to keep individual files under 100MB and a full repository under 500MB; compress very large .csv files as .gzip, and bundle other bulky material as .zip. Avoid linking to a GitHub repository that mixes your data and code together with unrelated software in the body of your article — machines cannot tell the two apart from a bare link, so cite the repository properly instead and let the reference list carry the URL.

**Naming.** Organize files into folders that reflect the structure of the project (e.g., separate folders per study, and separate `data`, `code`, `output`, `materials`, and `documentation` folders within each). Name files so that both a human and a machine can tell what they are: include a keyword such as `data`, `code`, `codebook`, or `output` in the file name (e.g., `study-01_data.csv`), use only lowercase letters, digits, underscores, and dashes (no spaces or special characters), and use leading zeroes for numbered files (`study-02` not `study-2`) so that files sort correctly. Folder and file names should match the terminology used in the manuscript (e.g., if the paper calls something "Study 1," the folder should too), so a re-user — human or machine — can link a repository component back to the right part of the paper.

**File formats.** Store data in open, non-proprietary formats such as .csv (comma-separated, UTF-8 encoded) rather than .txt, and avoid proprietary archive formats such as .rar. If raw data can only be produced by commercial software, keep the original files in a `raw` subfolder for the record, but also export an open-format version for reuse. In spreadsheets, avoid storing data across multiple tabs (use separate files instead), avoid merged cells and blank rows or columns, and never rely on cell color, comments, or hyperlinks to carry information that a re-user needs, since none of that survives being read into statistical software.

**Codebooks.** Every data file needs a codebook (also called a data dictionary): a document that lists, at minimum, each column's exact name and a plain-language label describing what it contains. Where relevant, also record the response options and their labels (e.g., `1 = strongly disagree; 5 = strongly agree`), the original question wording, how missing values are coded, and any coding instructions (such as which items need to be reverse-scored before computing a scale mean). Software such as SPSS, JASP, or Jamovi can store data and codebook together in one labelled file; otherwise, a simple spreadsheet or .csv table with one row per variable works well. Store the codebook as a spreadsheet or .csv file rather than as a Word document or PDF, since the latter cannot be reliably parsed by software. For a package that helps generate a machine-readable codebook automatically, see @arslan_how_2019.

**Tabular structure.** Keep data files "tidy": one header row, one variable per column, one observation per row, with no merged headers or notes scattered across the sheet. Column names should use only letters, digits, and underscores (e.g., `participant_id`, not `Participant ID`), stay under about 32 characters, and be descriptive rather than cryptic (`self_esteem_1` rather than `SE1`). Related columns should share a common prefix and consistent numbering (e.g., `panas_1`, `panas_2`, …), and no column or row should be entirely empty. Screen open-text fields for anything that could identify a participant (names, email addresses, IP addresses) before sharing.

None of this needs to be memorized in full — the underlying idea is simply that a repository organized this way can be understood by a script without guesswork, which is what ultimately makes data and code findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable in practice, rather than just in principle.

## Organizing Your Data and Code

Beyond the file- and folder-level practices above, it also helps to follow an established documentation protocol for the project as a whole. In general, I recommend the **TIER protocol**: <https://www.projecttier.org/tier-protocol/>, which sets out a standard structure for organizing the data, code, and documentation behind a project so that others (including your future self) can quickly find what they are looking for.

When you are organizing your code, **take great care to make sure that any personally identifying information in your data is stored safely**. Open science is great, but you are responsible to share data responsibly. This means that you need to **ask participants permission to share their data** in the informed consent form (a [useful  resource](https://www.uu.nl/en/research/research-data-management/guides/informed-consent-for-data-sharing) is the Research Data Management Support page of the University of Utrecht). Whenever you collect personal data, make sure you [handle this data responsibly](https://www.uu.nl/en/research/research-data-management/guides/handling-personal-data). Information specialists at your university library should be able to help.

## Archiving Your Data and Code

If you use GitHub for version control during a project (see the [computational reproducibility chapter](#sec-computationalreproducibility)), remember that GitHub is not designed to guarantee long-term data storage, and companies can change what they offer through their free services at any time. This makes it less suitable to rely on as the sole long-term link for a scientific article, because articles need to remain traceable for decades. For scientific publications, you will want to archive a stable copy in a long-term data repository, using the comparison above to pick the repository that best matches your needs (for example, Zenodo for anonymized projects with code, or a GDPR-compliant repository such as PsychArchives or DataverseNL for pseudonymized data). For a broader list of options, see PLOS's [list of recommended data repositories](http://journals.plos.org/plosone/s/data-availability#loc-recommended-repositories).

If you used GitHub during your project, most repositories that support GitHub integration make it straightforward to archive a snapshot: for example, Zenodo can be linked directly to a GitHub repository so that every new GitHub release automatically creates a matching, citable, DOI-archived snapshot on Zenodo (see [Zenodo's GitHub guide](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/archiving-a-github-repository/referencing-and-citing-content)). This gives you a version-controlled working copy on GitHub during the project, and a stable, permanently archived copy with a DOI at the point of publication.

A good moment to create this stable archived version is when your manuscript is accepted for publication. You can then add the resulting DOI to your manuscript as you check the proofs before publication. It is recommended to link to your materials using the **DOI** rather than a plain URL, because a DOI is a persistent identifier that keeps working even if a website address changes later.
